articles.title: Chinese writing developed square forms gradually, shaped by language, tools and tradition, analysis suggests
articles.description: A new historical analysis challenges the received wisdom as to why Chinese characters developed their distinctive square shapes. The work, published in the International Journal of Arts and Technology, argues that their shape resulted from interacting linguistic, technological and cultural factors rather than a single cause.

articles.title: The Vera Rubin Has Found Two More of the Milky Way's Dim Satellites
articles.description: The Vera Rubin Observatory has detected two more of the Milky Ways' dim, hard to see satellites. One is an ultra-faint dwarf galaxy, and one is a globular cluster. Each one is a missing piece of the puzzle in the Milky Way's merger history. By finding more of these satellites, our understanding of galaxy growth, and the role dark matter plays in it, will improve.

articles.title: To watch and watch for: Week of Nov. 1
articles.description: After a surely productive Halloweekend and the conclusion of Hoptoberfest always comes the onset of November and an imminent Thanksgiving. It is in between the spooky and the cuffing season that we find the rest of the genres neatly lined up for us to enjoy with friends and perhaps a dinner party to follow. If you're looking for an excuse to find reprieve from studying, a cozy JHMI read or an album to put on while getting ready in the morning, make sure to give this week's picks a chance! After premiering at the Venice International Film Festival this past September, the dark comedy spy thriller Wild Horse Nine is receiving its theatrical release this week. The film follows CIA agents Chris (John Malkovich) and Lee (Sam Rockwell) on their deployment to Easter Island shortly before the military coup that would install Pinochet as President. As they uncover more details about their past and present situations, things seem to keep throwing their plans sideways. The movie is both deeply pensive and hilariously funny with a notable standout performance to watch for from Malkovich, who received Best Actor at Venice for his role. With the NBA season's recent tipoff, talks about greatness, potential and unfortunately, injuries have already taken off in full force. Even with all of the talent on display in the modern league, players and fans alike must always remember the giants whose shoulders the present game of basketball stands on, and the legendary coach Phil Jackson won't let us forget that. In the book Masters of the Game, close friends Jackson and former sports journalist Sam Smith discuss the stories of the all-time best players and the details that make up basketball history, both on and off the court. Unfortunately for fans of Bearface's contemplative parts on songs like SUMMER, the singer has kept his head down since BROCKHAMPTON's breakup in 2022. However, this July, he released K-Bar under the name Ciarán and has since been teasing songs from his upcoming album Róisín ever since. For fans looking for introspective alternative RnB and brilliantly harmonized falsettos, this long-awaited return might be just the release to scratch your brain. Too often, music listeners are allowed to see music as a solitary act. Streaming services allow us to pipe music directly into our own ears and allow us to forget what recommending your favorite to your friends was like. Artist in Residence Xavier "Seven" Walker is combating this by presenting the Black album Frequency Sound Library, a listening room focused on community building and growing roots in the sounds of Baltimore. Pop by on Nov. 5 to join in on the process of cultural creation! As always, you can also check out the extended list below for even more recommendations! To watch… Wild Horse Nine - Nov. 6 Godzilla Minus Zero - Nov. 6 The Cat in the Hat - Nov. 6 Queen at Sea - Nov. 6 Paradise Lost - Nov. 6 To read… Masters of the Game, written by Sam Smith and Phil Jackson - Nov. 3 The Space Behind the Face, written by Robert Wilson with Keith McDermott - Nov. 3 The Sense of Sight - Nov. 3 Secret Daughter, written by Veronica Gonzalez Peña - Nov. 3 The Chessboard, written by Jean-Philippe Toussaint - Nov. 3 To listen… Roisin, by Ciaran Música Divino, by ericdoa - Nov. 3 Final Girl, by Dove Cameron - Nov. 6 Fresh, by Lil Baby - Nov. 6 SWALLOW!, by Shygirl - Nov. 6 Live events… Xavier Walker: Black Frequency Sound Library - Nov. 5 This event is free; registration is encouraged. 2026 Excellence in Undergraduate Writing Awards, with the University Writing Program at Johns Hopkins - Nov. 4 This event is free. Adam Johnson: Chaffee Visiting Writer - Nov. 4 Archive Fever & AI: Found Text and Creative Practice in the Age of Generative AI - Nov. 7 This event is free; registration is required. Luxury & Loss Opening Day Artist Talks, at the Walters Art Museum - Nov. 7

articles.title: An admission of unkindness
articles.description: I fear kindness the way a cat fears water. One touch of that gaudy mask, and I want to scurry away. The showy nature behind it all functions as a party of porcelain dolls at a masquerade, with each disguise telling me about the lies that obscure the person responsible. Mostly, I fear the kindness in my own false image. My mask is likely much more extensive than yours, despite my best efforts at authenticity. And I am yet to figure out all the lies I've told. You should know what I mean. The pressurized camaraderie found in tight-knit social circles. An unspoken rule more binding than law to declare your agreement. It's all rather cultish. And I think we're all leaders whether we realize it or not. Of course, some more than others. Religious and political leaders concealing sexual abuse cases are completely different from your next-door neighbor who sends yearly Christmas cards talking shit about you. Still, it's just shit hitting the ever-revolving fan. Yet you can't really know what I am referring to. Even after reading this article, you still won't fully understand what I mean. Right now, as I write in a moment of rare serenity, I can only see it vaguely. That is because we will never truly grasp the depth of our own unkindness. Don't worry. You are probably a good person, maybe even a kind person. I promise I am not some pessimist who views every act of kindness as some elaborate scheme to get somewhere in the world. But let's be real. We are all thinkers. I wonder what your most intrusive thoughts are now. Are you like me? Wondering how some people still don't know sidewalk etiquette. Cursing a mom with a stroller who passed you on a half-marathon. Okay, maybe you didn't do those two, but I still think we're similar. In these moments of occasional insincerity, which I'll discuss soon, I always felt a vague illness creeping down my spine. I used to see this as my guilty conscience, and though that is not technically wrong, a better descriptor for me would be my own moral disillusionment. Before I go more in-depth on my own acts of cruelty, I should explain that I grew up in rural Minnesota. It is important to preface this by saying this is just my experience, and what happened there happens everywhere. Still, the stereotype of Midwesterners having a "fake kindness" rang especially true to me. I recall teachers with affirmations on their doors gossiping about past students. Moms and Dads at the local golf course saying the darnedest things as one went to the restroom. Friends and foes offering up a favor that you would be damned to accept. All within a day. Of course, I was an active participant. I just did not realize it then. My environment, which I considered entirely artificial, made for an easy scapegoat. On top of this, people, specifically my teachers, always said I was kind. They told my parents, who would then tell me with pride what they had heard. Any negative action I ever did was met with a reminder that it was uncharacteristic, and at my core, I was a good, kind person. When a positive trait is constantly applied to you, it is easy to believe you are incapable of the opposite. I'm sure most people believe they are kind because they want to believe they are good. But I believed I was kind because I never considered I couldn't be. I started waking up when I moved to Baltimore. Yes. I was aware of certain moral imperfections beforehand; a genuine apology wasn't foreign, but living in a different region gave me a completely different context. Without an environment to blame, or people who cast me as the kind one, it was difficult to brush off the mean thoughts that ran through my head about strangers and the gossip I partook in. As I ruminated on my ethical inadequacies, I began to understand that a moral shortcoming was not equivalent to a mistake or a mess-up. It was just an essential piece in discovering that I am both unkind and kind. I have never been the worst person in the world. And frankly, I like to think that despite everything in this article, I am still good. I would bring up examples to reinforce that claim because I worry that I come across as so many other things right now, but that would be frustratingly counterintuitive. While I don't claim them as core values, I acknowledge that anything opposite of kindness can be a trait of mine under the wrong circumstances. I am frightened that I won't always come to this understanding. What will likely happen is I will feel morally superior because someone else in my life does something much worse than whisper a bratty rumor. I write this article as an awakening from a spell we will likely fall under again. It is a reminder, saying that we are all capable of cruelty. Matthew Bohnsack is a freshman from Moose Lake, Minn., majoring in English.
